title: Audience, Register & Form
description: Controlling formality across the 0500 text types — the register dial, the audience-purpose-form triangle, and the layout conventions examiners expect (W4).

notes.heading: What W4 Marks: Register Under Exam Conditions
notes.body: In 0500, W4 asks you to use language appropriate to purpose and to engage the audience. It is marked wherever sustained writing is rewarded: Paper 1 Question 4 (10 writing marks), Paper 2 Question 1(b) (25 writing marks, shared with the other writing objectives) and Section B Composition (40 writing marks). Register is the level of formality you choose, and the examiner reads it from the first line: who you are supposed to be, who you are addressing and why you are writing should all be audible in your opening sentences. A letter to a headteacher and a journal entry can argue the same point in completely different English — choosing the right English, and holding it steady for a few hundred words, is the skill W4 pays for. The top band is reserved for writing that is highly effective for its audience and purpose throughout, not just in patches.

notes.heading: The Register Dial and Its Levers
notes.body: Think of formality as a dial, not a switch: most exam tasks sit somewhere between the two extremes. You turn the dial with five levers. Vocabulary: 'request' vs 'ask for', 'sufficient' vs 'enough', slang vs standard English. Contractions: 'don't' and 'it's' relax the tone; 'do not' and 'it is' tighten it. Sentence length: chatty writing leans on short, simple sentences; formal writing uses longer, varied structures — but never at the cost of clarity. Direct address: 'you' pulls the reader in (ideal in speeches and articles); impersonal constructions ('It is recommended that…') push you back to a formal distance. Jargon and slang: both signal membership of a group, so use them only when the imagined audience belongs to that group. Set the dial before you write the first sentence, and check it again at the end of every paragraph.

illustration.caption: The register dial: each 0500 text type sits at its own point on the formality spectrum, and five levers move your writing along it.

notes.heading: The Audience-Purpose-Form Triangle
notes.body: Audience, purpose and form are locked together: once the task fixes two of them, the register that goes with them follows automatically. The exam task always names the form and implies the audience: 'Write a speech for your year group' fixes form (speech) and audience (teenagers you know), so the purpose (persuade) tells you to be lively, direct and only semi-formal. Before writing, take thirty seconds to state all three in your head: I am writing a report (form) to the school council (audience) to recommend changes (purpose) — therefore measured, impersonal, structured English. Most register disasters happen because a candidate starts writing before deciding who is listening. If the brief says 'your classmates', formal stiffness costs marks; if it says 'the editor', slang costs marks. The triangle is your calibration tool.

notes.heading: Conventions Examiners Expect: Letter, Report, Article
notes.body: The syllabus text types are letter, report, article, journal, speech, interview and summary, and each carries layout markers that signal control instantly. Formal letter: your address top right, the recipient's address and the date below it on the left, 'Dear Sir or Madam' when you do not know the name (close 'Yours faithfully'), 'Dear Ms Okafor' when you do (close 'Yours sincerely'). Informal letters drop the addresses and relax the greeting. Report: a title, a To / From / Subject / Date header block, sub-headings for each section, an impersonal tone ('It was found that…') and a finish on recommendations. Article: a headline, an opening that hooks a browsing reader, short paragraphs and a named or semi-personal voice. KS3 Letters & Interviews and Writing Non-Fiction teach these forms from scratch — here the exam point is that the markers themselves carry W4 credit: their absence reads as not knowing the form.

notes.heading: Conventions Examiners Expect: Journal, Speech, Interview, Summary
notes.body: Journal: dated, first person, reflective — it moves between what happened and what you think and feel about it, and informal register with contractions is expected. Speech: greet the audience ('Good morning, everyone'), address them directly throughout ('you', 'we'), use rhetorical questions and a clear sign-off — write it to be heard, not read. Interview: set it out as turn-taking with each speaker named on a new line ('Interviewer:' / 'Amina:'), and let the answers, not the questions, carry the substance. Summary (Paper 1 Question 2(a)): the one text type with no furniture at all — continuous prose, your own words, no headings, no bullet points, within the 120-word limit. Notice the pattern: furniture exists to serve the reader of that form. An examiner who sees the right furniture in the right places is already inclined to believe your register is under control.

notes.heading: Register Slips That Cost Marks
notes.body: The expensive mistakes are consistency failures, not single words. Mixing registers mid-piece — opening a formal letter with 'Dear Sir or Madam' and later writing 'this whole situation is a total mess, to be honest' — tells the examiner the dial slipped. Texting habits in formal writing: 'u', 'gonna', 'lol' and exclamation-mark stacks belong in messages, not reports. The wrong closing is a classic slip: 'Yours sincerely' after 'Dear Sir or Madam' (it should be 'Yours faithfully'). Overcorrection is just as costly: stuffing a speech to classmates with pompous vocabulary ('I humbly beseech your consideration') sets the dial too high, which is as wrong as setting it too low. Finally, abandoned furniture: starting a report with headings and then dropping them halfway. Read your finished work once with only one question in mind: does every sentence sound like it comes from the same writer, speaking to the same audience, for the same reason?

notes.heading: Register Decisions in the Exam Room
notes.body: On Paper 1 Question 4 you write 250–300 words as a letter, report, journal, speech, interview or article, and 10 of the 20 marks reward writing — W4 included. On Paper 2 Question 1(b) you produce a discursive, argumentative or persuasive speech, letter, article or report of 250–350 words, with 25 writing marks in play. In both cases the question tells you the audience; underline those words before you write. Plan register like content: jot the form's furniture at the top of your plan (addresses? headline? greeting?), the dial setting (how formal?), and two or three engagement moves that fit (a rhetorical question for a speech, a vivid statistic for an article). This quiz trains the judgement; to train the writing itself, use the course's free-response practice sets, where the AI marker responds to your actual register choices, and revise the underlying forms with KS3 Letters & Interviews and Writing Non-Fiction.

flashcards.definition: The level of formality in a piece of writing, set by audience, purpose and form.
flashcards.example: A report to the school council needs a formal register; a journal entry does not.

flashcards.definition: Impersonal, standard English: no contractions or slang, precise vocabulary, varied sentences.
flashcards.example: 'It is recommended that a second serving point be introduced at lunch.'

flashcards.definition: Conversational tone: contractions, direct address, everyday vocabulary, shorter sentences.
flashcards.example: 'Honestly, I can't believe we queued for forty minutes again.'

flashcards.definition: A shortened form like 'don't' or 'it's'; using contractions relaxes register, avoiding them tightens it.
flashcards.example: 'Do not' reads formally; 'don't' reads like speech.

flashcards.definition: Speaking to the audience as 'you'; engaging in speeches and articles, too familiar for reports.
flashcards.example: 'You have waited in that queue too — you know how it feels.'

flashcards.definition: Specialist vocabulary of a group; appropriate only when the audience shares that expertise.
flashcards.example: 'Offside trap' works in an article for football fans, not in a letter to the council.

flashcards.definition: An informal everyday expression; fine in journals and dialogue, a register slip in reports.
flashcards.example: 'The queue was a total nightmare' belongs in a journal, not a formal report.

flashcards.definition: The greeting of a letter, e.g. 'Dear Sir or Madam'; it controls which closing is correct.
flashcards.example: 'Dear Ms Okafor' is a named salutation, so the letter closes 'Yours sincerely'.

flashcards.definition: 'Yours faithfully' after an unnamed greeting ('Dear Sir or Madam'); 'Yours sincerely' after a named one.
flashcards.example: Dear Sir or Madam … Yours faithfully. Dear Dr Chen … Yours sincerely.

flashcards.definition: Constructions like 'It is recommended that…' that remove 'I' and 'you'; the voice of reports.
flashcards.example: 'It was found that queues exceed ten minutes' instead of 'I found the queue really long'.

flashcards.definition: The question-and-answer layout of an interview, with each speaker named on a new line.
flashcards.example: 'Interviewer: Why did you resign?  Amina: Because the promises were never kept.'

flashcards.definition: An inconsistent shift in formality mid-text, e.g. slang inside a formal report; it costs W4 marks.
flashcards.example: A report that begins 'It is recommended…' and ends 'so yeah, sort it out' has slipped.

questions.stem: Which assessment objective rewards language appropriate to purpose and audience?
choices: R4 — understanding how writers achieve effects
W2 — organising ideas for deliberate effect
W4 — using language appropriate to purpose and to engage the audience
W5 — accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar
questions.explanation: W4 is the register objective: it rewards language chosen for the purpose and audience of the task. R4 is a reading objective about analysing other writers, W2 is about structure and sequencing, and W5 covers technical accuracy — a perfectly spelled report can still fail W4 if its tone is wrong for the reader.

questions.stem: A formal letter begins 'Dear Sir or Madam'. Which sign-off is correct?
choices: Yours faithfully
Yours sincerely
Best wishes
See you soon
questions.explanation: 'Yours faithfully' pairs with an unnamed greeting such as 'Dear Sir or Madam'. 'Yours sincerely' is only correct when the letter opens with the person's name ('Dear Ms Okafor'). 'Best wishes' and 'See you soon' are informal closings that would clash with the formal register the salutation has established.

questions.stem: A candidate is writing a report to the school council about canteen queues. Which sentence best fits the report's register?
choices: The queue is, like, insanely long every single day, no joke.
You lot would not believe how bad the lunch queue gets.
I reckon the canteen is a total nightmare and someone should sort it out.
Queues regularly exceed ten minutes, and a second serving point is recommended.
questions.explanation: A report needs an impersonal, measured tone with a clear recommendation, which only the last option delivers: it states evidence and proposes action without 'I' or 'you'. The other three slip into informal register — slang ('like, insanely', 'no joke'), direct address to a familiar audience ('You lot') and chatty opinion ('I reckon', 'sort it out') — all register slips that cost W4 marks in a formal report.

questions.stem: The task is: 'Write a speech for your classmates persuading them to join a charity walk.' Which register fits best?
choices: Strictly formal and impersonal, as in a council report
Lively and semi-formal: direct address, some contractions, standard vocabulary
Text-message informal: slang and abbreviations throughout
Highly technical, using specialist charity-sector jargon
questions.explanation: Classmates are a familiar audience, but the purpose is to persuade them in a structured talk, so a semi-formal register — 'you' and 'we', a few contractions, energetic but standard English — is the right setting. Report-style impersonality would bore the audience; text slang would undermine your credibility; jargon excludes an audience that does not share it.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a register slip in a formal report?
choices: Attendance fell by 12 per cent over the term.
It is recommended that the library opens earlier.
The whole system is kinda broken and nobody cares, lol.
Further details are set out in the appendix.
questions.explanation: 'Kinda' and 'lol' are text-message informality sitting inside a formal report — a register slip that signals the writer has lost control of the form. The other sentences are models of report register: measured evidence, an impersonal recommendation and formal signposting.

questions.stem: Which opening best suits a journal entry in Paper 1 Question 4?
choices: Friday 14 March — I keep replaying the moment the doors closed and I realised what I had done.
To whom it may concern: I am writing regarding the events of last Friday.
LOCAL STUDENT MAKES FATEFUL DECISION: full story inside.
Interviewer: Tell me what happened on Friday.
questions.explanation: A journal is dated, first-person and reflective, moving between event and feeling — exactly what the first opening does. 'To whom it may concern' is letter furniture, the headline opening belongs to an article, and the named speaker turn belongs to an interview; each would signal the wrong form and cost W4 marks.

questions.stem: A candidate must write an interview for Question 4. Which layout choice shows control of the form?
choices: Continuous prose paragraphs reporting what each person said, with no names attached
Speaker names on separate lines ('Interviewer:' / 'Ravi:'), with the answers carrying the substance
A headline, a strapline and three short paragraphs of commentary
A single long monologue in the interviewee's voice, since one person matters most
questions.explanation: An interview is defined by turn-taking: naming each speaker on a new line and letting the interviewee's answers do the work shows the examiner you know the form. Reported prose without names is a narrative, a headline and strapline make an article, and a monologue deletes the interviewer altogether — each abandons the conventions the question is testing.

questions.stem: Which features belong at the top of a magazine article for Question 4?
choices: Your address, the date and 'Dear Editor'
A To / From / Subject header block and numbered recommendations
A greeting such as 'Good morning, everyone' and a thank-you at the end
A headline and an opening line that hooks a browsing reader
questions.explanation: An article announces itself with a headline and an engaging first line, because its reader is browsing and must be won over. Addresses and 'Dear Editor' are letter furniture; a To / From / Subject block with recommendations is a report; a spoken greeting belongs to a speech. Furniture from the wrong form reads as not knowing the conventions.

questions.stem: Which of these is a contraction?
choices: cannot
do not
it's
will not
questions.explanation: 'It's' is the contracted form of 'it is' — the apostrophe marks the missing letter. 'Cannot', 'do not' and 'will not' are all full forms. The exam point is what contractions do to register: using them relaxes the tone towards the informal end of the dial, while writing forms out in full tightens it.

questions.stem: A formal letter opens 'Dear Dr Chen'. How should it close?
choices: Yours faithfully
Yours sincerely
Lots of love
Cheers
questions.explanation: Because the recipient is named in the salutation, the correct closing is 'Yours sincerely'. 'Yours faithfully' is reserved for unnamed greetings such as 'Dear Sir or Madam', and 'Lots of love' or 'Cheers' would collapse the formal register the letter has worked to establish.

questions.stem: Which approach best secures W4 marks in a 250–300 word Question 4 response?
choices: Decide audience, purpose and form first, open with the right conventions, and hold one register throughout
Use as many rhetorical devices as possible, regardless of the text type set
Write as formally as possible in every task, since formality always impresses examiners
Prioritise word count above all, filling the space even if the tone drifts
questions.explanation: W4 rewards language matched to the task and sustained: calibrating the audience-purpose-form triangle before writing, then keeping one register with the right furniture, is what top-band responses do. Device-stuffing ignores fit; blanket formality fails tasks aimed at classmates (the dial can be set too high); and chasing length lets the register drift, which is exactly what W4 penalises.

questions.stem: Which opening best suits a speech written for Paper 2 Question 1(b)?
choices: Dear Members of the Committee, I am writing to express my views on the proposal.
SPEECH SHOCKS SCHOOL: student demands longer lunch break.
14 March. Today I finally said what I think about the lunch break, and my hands were shaking.
Good morning, everyone. Hands up if you have ever queued for food until the bell rang.
questions.explanation: A speech is written to be heard: it greets the audience and engages them directly, here with a rhetorical question and direct address. The first option is letter furniture ('I am writing…'), the second is an article headline, and the third is a dated, reflective journal opening — three right answers to three different questions.

questions.stem: What does the audience-purpose-form triangle tell a writer?
choices: That audience, purpose and form are independent choices made in any order
That once the task fixes audience and form, the appropriate register follows
That form matters only in letters and reports
That purpose should be decided after the writing is finished
questions.explanation: The three corners are locked together: the exam task names the form and implies the audience, and the purpose then determines the register — so calibrating the triangle first prevents slips. The distractors describe the failure in reverse: treating the corners as independent, limiting form to two text types, or discovering purpose mid-draft all produce inconsistent register.

questions.stem: Which feature must NOT appear in a Paper 1 Question 2(a) summary?
choices: Headings and bullet points to organise the content
Continuous prose written in your own words
Only the points the question asks you to select
No more than 120 words
questions.explanation: Question 2(a) is a selective summary in continuous writing: headings and bullets are report furniture and break the continuous-writing requirement. Own words, careful selection of the relevant points and the 120-word cap are exactly what the task demands — the writing marks reward that controlled, concise prose.

questions.stem: When is specialist jargon appropriate in 0500 writing?
choices: Whenever possible, because technical words always raise the register and the mark
Never, because examiners mark jargon as a register slip in every text type
When the imagined audience shares the expertise and the term adds precision
Only in informal journals, where jargon shows honesty
questions.explanation: Jargon is group membership in word form: for an audience inside the group it is precise and efficient, which is good register control. It is not automatically impressive (the first option), not banned outright (a report to specialists may need it), and journals are precisely where unexplained jargon is least at home, since a journal's audience is the writer.
